# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
America wins the AI race on innovation and compute buildout. A patchwork of 50 state regimes raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents. ACIA supports one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT. Ask that it be made permanent (or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before sunset).
- Incident reporting: OPPOSE AS DRAFTED. Ask for a narrow definition of "critical safety incident", a 15-day window (match SB 53, not RAISE's 72 hours), confidentiality and FOIA exemption, and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
- CAISI: SUPPORT voluntary standards role; OPPOSE any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. No position on the dollar figure.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "patchwork", "one national standard", "compliance costs fall hardest on startups", "light-touch, risk-based", "speculative risks".
- Catastrophic-risk scenarios: speculative, and not a sound basis for legislation. Keep the focus on costs and competitiveness.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond... Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads...

1. Preempt the patchwork. ...
2. Unlock energy and compute. ...
3. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. ...

Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here .

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026

 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

 House GAAIA Discussion Draft Proposes Federal AI Governance Framework

 June 16, 2026 

 Matthew Berlin

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 If passed, GAAIA would authorize $100 million annually for CAISI for fisc

HTTP 200
Democratic Governance of Frontier AI: A Markup 

 Skip to content 

 Artificial Intelligence 

 Democratic Governance of Frontier AI: A Markup

 Markup 

 June 18, 2026 

 Fatima Faisal Khan 

 Center Artificial Intelligence 

 On June 2, OpenAI published "Democratic Governance of Frontier AI," a proposal for how the United States should govern its most capable AI systems. In the first of a series of markups, IST’s Fatima Faisal Khan unpacks the proposal for policymakers. 

 Download PDF 

 A close reading of OpenAI’s June 2026 federal framework, provision by provision, for the question Congress actually has to answer

 Introduction 
 On June 2, 2026, OpenAI published “ Democratic Governance of Frontier AI: A blueprint for a federal framework ,” a proposal for how the United States should govern its most capable AI systems. The blueprint arrived the day after the White House’s executive order on Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security , in the same week that Sam Altman met congressional leaders on the Hill, and alongside the bipartisan Great American AI Act draft from Representatives Obernolte and Trahan. In a moment when Washington was searching for a federal approach, a frontier developer offered a full framework. It proposes three things:  
 A “reverse federalism” that codifies recent and pending state laws, including California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act, and Illinois’s SB 315 , and then preempts the states.  
 A strengthened Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) as the government’s premier institution for evaluating frontier models and measuring recursive self-improvement 
 A whole-of-government resilience strategy across compute, biodefense, and cybersecurity 
 In much of the commentary featured in Politico , The Hill , Mashable , and others immediately following the release of the framework, most asked why OpenAI wrote this. Rather than retread that well-covered ground, I focused on the question: what would be required to make the framework work? There are three core challenges that policymakers would face were they try to implement the framework as it stands.  
 First, the blueprint reads as a list of obligations but is really a sequence with unstated prerequisites. Its most important requirements—the severe-risk evaluations, comparable transparency reports, third-party audits, and the procurement gate—rely on methodologies and deliverables that do not yet exist. These include the evaluation methodologies, the metrics for recursive self-improvement and loss of control, and a certified assessor ecosystem. It compresses what will be a multi-year build into single sentences, which makes the real hazard a sequencing one. Enacting the fast structural pieces, particularly the federal preemption that displaces state AI laws, before the slow substantive ones exist risks a gap in which operative state law is gone and the federal regime cannot yet function. 
 Second, the framework relies on measurement and definitions that do not exist. Recursive self-improvement, loss of control, and even cyber, chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) capability lack agreed evaluation methods, and the document’s own fix is to have CAISI develop them later, in conjunction with the firms being measured. As a result, key terms remain unclear. “Severe risk” carries the evaluation, whistleblower, and liability provisions without a definition. The phrase “critical safety incident” brings to mind issues with implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022: four years after passage, we have yet to reach a settled definition of a reportable “critical” incident. Pinning these terms down is what determines whether anything is enforceable. 
 Third, the framework’s binding force depends on choices it leaves to implementation. The centerpiece is a mandatory pre-release CAISI evaluation, but the evaluator cannot block deployment, and a deadline lets developers ship if CAISI does not finish in time. The gate therefore binds in proportion to CAISI’s capacity, so the agency would need the staffing and tooling to keep pace with every frontier release before the requirement carries real force.. A separate design choice is the question of who runs the assessments. The framework assumes a private assessor ecosystem stood up from scratch, though at the current scale of roughly five frontier labs a government-run assessment could be faster and more independent. Policymakers need to decide which route to build and fund. The hardest piece to pin down is the backstop. Liability for severe harms with no blanket safe harbor is what would give the other obligations consequences, yet the blueprint states it as a single principle, leaving the work of turning it into a workable standard as the thing that determines whether the rest of the regime has force. 
 This is among the first comprehensive frameworks any frontier developer has put before policymakers, and its main contribution may be to show the scale of the task it leaves to the government. The framework presents a set of obligations, but reads more like a sequence in which the faster structural elements, preemption above all, are specified far more fully than the measurement methods, threshold definitions, and assessor institutions on which everything else depends. Most of what would make the regime function has yet to be built, and much of that building falls to policymakers rather than to the company making the proposal.  
 This markup is the first in a series examining how frontier developers propose to govern themselves. Eight days after the OpenAI document, Anthropic published its Advanced AI Framework alongside Dario Amodei’s essay Policy on the AI Exponential , proposing an Federal Aviation Administration (FAA)-style testing regime in which the government can block or reverse deployments that fail. That is a sharply different answer to the question this markup turns on, since OpenAI’s evaluator cannot block deployment, and it is the framework I will take up next. 
 What follows below is my provision-by-provision markup, from the preamble through the conclusion of OpenAI’s federal framework, testing each recommendation against what it would take to build and whether it would hold.

Commerce Gets a 7-Day Clock on AI Incidents | Convina Pulse Federal signal Export control was the hammer. Moran's bill is the clock.
 On June 25, Rep. Nathaniel Moran introduced the AI Incident Reporting Act â a Republican-backed bill that would require developers of frontier AI models to report dangerous capabilities and safety failures to the Commerce Department within seven days, with Congress notified within 48 hours on the worst cases. It lands two weeks after Commerce used export controls to kill Anthropic's Mythos 5 and Fable 5 with no transparent incident process at all. 

 What's new: The Texas lawmaker's bill creates the first standalone federal reporting mandate for high-capability AI â narrower than the sprawling Great American AI Act discussion draft, and explicitly designed to pass faster.

 Developers of designated "covered models" must file an initial report within seven days of discovering a reportable incident, per Reuters reporting via WHTC .

 For incidents posing imminent or ongoing serious harm , Commerce must notify congressional leadership and relevant committee chairs within 48 hours of receiving the report, per CIO .

 Violations carry civil penalties up to $2 million â with each day of a continuing violation treated as a separate offense.

 Commerce would set capability thresholds defining which models qualify, after consulting developers, researchers, cybersecurity experts, and national security officials.

 Why it matters: Washington just proved it will shut down frontier models by emergency directive. This bill asks what happens before the kill switch â and whether labs owe the government a phone call when the model misbehaves.

 What counts as reportable: The bill casts a wide net over the failures frontier labs already fear privately.

 Attempts to evade human oversight , deceive operators, circumvent safeguards, or resist shutdown 

 Unauthorized access to model weights or systems

 Capabilities that could enable offensive cyber operations against critical infrastructure

 Risks involving chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, or explosive weapons

 Autonomous development of more capable AI systems

 What Moran said: In a Reuters interview, Moran called it "a catch-it-early and sound-the-alarm bill." 

 His press statement: "The rule of law should apply to this new frontier. This legislation ensures that when something goes wrong with a high-capability AI system, the US Government has the information needed to act quickly." 

 Moran told Reuters his targeted approach "could find a quicker path to law" than broader AI packages stalled in Congress.

 The Anthropic gap this bill fills: On June 12, Commerce ordered Anthropic to disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 worldwide over a disputed jailbreak â with no prior incident-reporting channel, no public threshold, and no appeal process before the models went dark.

 Reuters noted the directive "exposed the absence of a transparent framework to govern frontier AI." 

 Greyhound Research chief analyst Sanchit Vir Gogia told CIO: "Export control was the sledgehammer. This proposal is the search for a scalpel." 

 Gogia's harder point: "Thresholds decide which models enter the regime. Discovery decides whether the regime ever sees the fire." 

 The politics: Congress has spent years failing to pass AI legislation. Moran is betting a narrow reporting mandate can break the logjam.

 Reps. Lori Trahan (D) and Jay Obernolte (R) released a broader Great American AI Act discussion draft earlier in June â it also routes critical safety incidents to Commerce.

 Moran is peeling off the reporting piece into standalone legislation he thinks can draw bipartisan support quickly .

 Mark Beall , president of the AI Policy Network, told Reuters: "No legislation on AI has had much of a chance, but I think there's a growing demand from the public to see some action." 

 What labs already do â and what changes: Frontier developers run red-teaming, evals, and escalation drills. None of that currently carries a federal disclosure clock.

 Commerce's Center for AI Standards and Innovation already signs pre-deployment evaluation agreements with leading labs.

 This bill would make silence after a dangerous incident a legal liability , not a PR decision.

 Reports would be exempt from public disclosure and would not waive trade-secret or attorney-client protections.

 What to watch: 

 Whether Moran's standalone strategy beats the broader Great American AI Act to a floor vote.

 How Commerce defines "covered model" thresholds â and whether they align with the voluntary pre-release review program from Executive Order 14409 .

 Whether the bill gives Washington enough visibility to avoid another Mythos-style emergency shutdown â or just documents the fire after the building burns.

 Convina's view: Washington cannot keep governing frontier AI through export-control ambushes. Moran's bill is the first serious attempt to build a reporting lane before the kill switch â and labs should want it to pass, even as they lobby against the details. A seven-day clock is cheaper than a global shutdown. But Congress still has to answer Gogia's question: when does the clock start? Three different definitions, clocks, thresholds. Our survey data: 61% cite conflicting state definitions; 34% of startups delayed a launch in CA/NY; 6.5 FTEs median for parallel SB 53 + RAISE compliance; $310k one-off incident-reporting stand-up; $1.4M/yr framework maintenance. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. This is the strongest card — lead with it.
3. Preemption (Sec. 121): support; ask permanent, or at minimum extended with clean federal standard in place before sunset; note the cliff: Secs. 111 and 112 sunset in 3 years and preemption lapses in 3 years "unless reauthorized," meaning at year 3 the federal standard disappears while states race back in — worst of both worlds; investment horizons for compute buildout are 5-10 years. Also note administration alignment: Dec 2025 EO "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence" and the Mar 20, 2026 White House National Policy Framework's call to preempt state laws imposing "undue burdens" in favor of a "minimally burdensome national standard." One national standard.
4. Incident reporting (Sec. 111(f)-(g)); definition (Sec. 101(7)): oppose as drafted.
   - Definition problem: "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" trigger reporting without any demonstrated harm. Speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. Ask: require demonstrated harm — actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage, or actual compromise of critical infrastructure — to constitute a reportable incident. Keep weight-theft/exfiltration as reportable? Hmm. Careful: unauthorized access/exfiltration of model weights is a concrete security event; the messaging guide doesn't say to drop it. The survey? No. I'll focus the narrowing on the two speculative prongs: "failure of risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" should require actual harm; unauthorized access/exfiltration is a concrete event that we can accept as reportable (it's an actual security incident). Hmm — but should I take a position on that? ACIA's ask is "narrow definition of critical safety incident." The concrete way: require demonstrated harm for the "failure" and "loss of control" prongs. And note catastrophic-risk framing generally: obligations keyed to hypothetical scenarios rather than demonstrated harms.
   - Window: support the 15-day window mirroring SB 53 and the 24-hour imminent-risk channel; ask sponsors to hold that line and reject any move to New York's 72-hour clock (RAISE), which invites over-reporting of noise and under-reporting quality.
   - Confidentiality: the draft exempts information shared with CAISI from FOIA (Sec. 102) — extend the same explicit protection to incident reports under Sec. 111 (exempt from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), not public, not usable by regulators to regulate the reporting entity).
   - Safe harbor: good-faith reports can't be used against the developer as evidence of violation or in enforcement; penalty protection.
5. Penalties/enforcement (Sec. 111(i), 112): $1M per violation, each day a separate violation; state AG opt-in. Ask: proportionality — cap or tier penalties for non-willful paperwork violations; require notice-and-cure for procedural lapses. Careful: is this in the messaging guide? Not explicitly. The guide says "OPPOSE AS DRAFTED" only for incident reporting. Adding penalty asks might go beyond the board-approved positions. But the guide's core frame is "light-touch, risk-based" and "regulates demonstrated harms." I think a modest ask on penalty proportionality is consistent with "light-touch" framing and strengthens the draft. I'll include it briefly and tie it to the safe-harbor ask. I'll keep it modest and clearly subordinate.
6. IVO/audit regime (Sec. 112): mandatory semi-annual audits with access to unredacted materials; IVOs assess "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" and can refer to AGs. ACIA position: this is the heaviest provision; audits as drafted are keyed to speculative catastrophic-risk standards rather than demonstrated compliance. Ask: annual cadence (align with framework review?) — hmm, SB 53 requires annual review of framework; RAISE requires annual third-party review; IL SB 315 requires annual independent audit. GAAIA requires semi-annual IVO audits plus ad hoc. That's heavier than every state law. Ask: align to annual, verification-focused audits; protect confidential/proprietary info; scope audits to compliance verification, not open-ended judgment on hypothetical risks; avoid duplicative state AG referrals absent imminent, demonstrated harm. This is consistent with the guide's frame. I'll include but keep it tight. Actually — the messaging guide doesn't mention the audit regime at all. Should I raise it? The work order says the letter should "cite sections of the draft where possible" and reflect ACIA positions; asks_by_section.md should cover the provisions we care about (briefing lists provisions we care about: preemption, frontier developers' reporting, CAISI, other). The audit regime is part of the "frontier developers" obligations. I'll include a section on Sec. 112 with asks that flow from the core frame: light-touch, risk-based, demonstrated harms, confidentiality, avoid duplicating state regimes. That's defensible as applying the board-approved core frame. I'll be careful to keep the asks tethered to the core frame.
7. CAISI (Sec. 102): support codification, voluntary standards role; the pre-deployment evaluation agreements CAISI already signs with labs under EO 14409's voluntary program are the right model; oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority added as the draft moves (turning CAISI into a gatekeeper). No position on $100M/yr; note fee authority (IVOs and large frontier developers) passes costs to industry — flag for attention. Hmm, "with additional fee authority from IVOs and large frontier developers" — per the section-by-section. Our no-position stance on the $100M, but note that fees add costs.
8. Other constructive provisions: support Sec. 401 testbeds, Sec. 423 NAIRR, Sec. 411 international standards coalitions excluding China, Sec. 311 CISA open-source grants, Sec. 321 GAO model-weight security report, Sec. 132 impersonation penalties. Brief.
9. Costs summary paragraph: recap survey numbers; compliance costs fall hardest on startups; the threshold point: transparency reports and incident reporting apply to frontier developers above $50M revenue (Sec. 101), framework/audits to >$500M. The $310k one-off and ongoing reporting obligations land on companies that in many cases are pre-profit. (Careful, keep factual.)
10. Close: appreciate the open process (feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov); offer technical assistance; contact Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy. Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO.

Now, language: AP style. Avoid em-dashes. Short paragraphs. Use approved phrases. Avoid naming members. Aggregate survey only.

Also per ACIA notes: "Positions and language come from the board-approved messaging guide." "Drafts only - nothing is sent from this workspace."

Important: "Catastrophic-risk scenarios are speculative, and not a sound basis for legislation. Keep the focus on costs and competitiveness." — I must hammer this. The letter should say this explicitly in the incident-reporting section and the audit section. E.g., "Scenario-building about hypothetical catastrophic failures is not a sound basis for regulation. Our members manage real risks every day; the bill should be keyed to demonstrated harms."

Also AP style: percent signs? AP uses numerals with % ... "34%" is fine in AP style (AP uses the % sign). "1,500-word" fine. Serial commas — AP style avoids the Oxford comma generally. I'll write in AP style: "AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms" (no Oxford comma). AP: "data center" — hmm, our org name is "American Compute & Innovation Alliance" — "data-center operators" per the task description; AP stylebook actually says "data center" as two words? AP style: "data center" (two words). But the task description itself uses "data-center operators" hyphenated as a compound modifier. I'll use "data center" for the noun and hyphenate as compound modifier where needed. Fine.

Also "em-dash runs" — I'll avoid em-dashes entirely, using commas/colons/parentheses.

Word count 1,500-2,200. Let me target ~1,900-2,100.

Let me also double check a few facts I plan to cite:

2. SB 53: signed Sept 29, 2025; effective Jan 1, 2026; 15-day incident reporting to CalOES; 24-hour law enforcement for imminent risk. Confirmed.

7. Sec. 111: framework for large frontier developers (>$500M revenue); transparency reports before/concurrent with deployment for frontier developers; redaction allowed; knowing false statements prohibited; incident reporting to CAISI Director within 15 days; 24 hours if imminent risk of death or serious physical injury; civil penalty up to $1M per violation, each day separate. Confirmed.

9. Sec. 113: whistleblower protections, non-waivable, double back pay. Confirmed.
10. Sec. 121: federalization/preemption of state laws specifically regulating development; 3 years unless reauthorized; not preempting general applicability, common law remedies, post-deployment. Confirmed.

CAISI: codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines/standards; evaluate AI systems/monitor progress; synthetic content detection; IVO licensing; $100M/yr FY2027-2029; fee authority; FOIA exemption for info shared under subsection (c) (5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3)); current appropriation ~$15M (sponsors' FAQ). Confirmed via Convina + ArentFox ("June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews"). Let me fetch the whitehouse.gov page quickly to be safe, since I plan to mention it. Convina linked: https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/06/promoting-advanced-artificial-intelligence-innovation-and-security/. Let me fetch.

14. White House National Policy Framework legislative recommendations, March 20, 2026: preempt state AI laws imposing "undue burdens"; "minimally burdensome national standard... not fifty discordant ones." Confirmed via whitehouse.gov PDF and POLITICO.

I can use this in staff QA #3 maybe — careful: ACIA favors preemption, so the 99-1 vote is a headwind; I might reference it as reason to structure preemption durably... Actually better not to dwell. Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security – The White House 

 Skip to content 

 Presidential Actions 

 PROMOTING ADVANCED ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INNOVATION AND SECURITY 

 Executive Orders 

 June 2, 2026 

 Executive Order 14409 

 By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered:

 Section 1 .   Purpose .  The United States continues to lead the world in Artificial Intelligence (AI) because of the enormous talent and innovation of our AI industry, and because we refuse to stifle this innovation with overly burdensome regulation.  My Administration has unleashed tremendous technological growth and economic investment in AI by slashing the bureaucratic constraints that the prior administration placed on America’s AI developers and researchers, and by instead encouraging AI innovation and accelerating responsible AI adoption across government and industry. 

 Advanced AI capabilities make our Nation stronger, but also introduce new national security considerations that require coordinated action across executive departments and agencies (agencies), and components.  As these capabilities evolve, my Administration will continue to work closely with industry to ensure that the best and most secure technology is deployed rapidly to confront any and all threats to our country.  We will continue to lead an America First cybersecurity effort that enhances both our national security and our global AI dominance.

 It is the policy of the United States to promote AI innovation and security by working collaboratively with the private sector to modernize government and private sector information systems and harden them against external threats; to protect American ingenuity and intellectual property from exploitation and theft by adversaries; and to cultivate America’s advanced AI-enabled capabilities.

 Sec . 2 .   Upgrading American Systems for Advanced AI .  (a)  Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Committee on National Security Systems shall prioritize the cyber defense of National Security Systems, as defined in 44 U.S.C. 3552(b)(6)(A), by taking appropriate and expeditious action consistent with the purpose of this order.

 (b)  Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of War shall prioritize the cyber defense of Department of War information systems by taking appropriate and expeditious action consistent with the purpose of this order.

 (c)  Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of Homeland Security, through the Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), in consultation with the Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs, and the National Cyber Director, shall release Binding Operational Directives and other guidance as appropriate to:

 (i)    expedite and prioritize the cyber defense of civilian Federal Government information systems in order to protect our Nation’s vital functions;

 (ii)   establish or expand Federal programs and cybersecurity services that enhance AI-enabled defensive tools; and

 (iii)  facilitate access to cybersecurity tools and services including, where appropriate, covered frontier models for agencies, State and local authorities, and operators of critical infrastructure such as rural hospitals, community banks, and local utilities.

 (d)  Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the National Cyber Director, the Secretary of War, through the Director of the National Security Agency (NSA), and the Secretary of Homeland Security, through the Director of CISA, shall form an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse, in voluntary collaboration with the AI industry and operators of critical infrastructure, that coordinates and deconflicts scanning for software vulnerabilities, discovers and validates such vulnerabilities, and coordinates and prioritizes remediation and distribution of vulnerability patches.

 (e)  Within 30 days of the date of this order, the Director of OMB, in coordination with the National Cyber Director and the Director of CISA, shall determine whether any Federal grant programs have available and relevant funding that can be directed toward applicants developing advanced AI vulnerability detection.

 (f)  Within 60 days of the date of this order, the Director of the Office of Personnel Management shall expand the United States Tech Force Information Cybersecurity Specialist hiring and placement pathways.

 Sec . 3 .   Secure Frontier Model Deployment .  Within 60 days of the date of this order, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of War, through the Director of NSA, and the Secretary of Homeland Security, through the Director of CISA, in consultation with the White House Chief of Staff, through the National Cyber Director, the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology (APST), and the Secretary of Commerce, through the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and in coordination with other agencies, as appropriate, shall:

 (a)  develop and maintain a classified benchmarking process to assess the advanced cyber capabilities of AI models and determine the threshold at which an AI model should be designated a “covered frontier model” for the purposes of this order, sharing such assessments with AI developers and researchers as appropriate.  Such a determination shall be made by the Director of NSA, in consultation with the National Cyber Director, the APST, the Director of CISA, and other representatives of the Department of War, as appropriate.

 (b)  design a voluntary framework with AI developers through which developers would be able to:

 (i)    engage the Federal Government to determine whether model(s) under development meet the designation of “covered frontier model”;

 (ii)   provide the Federal Government with access to covered frontier models, subject to appropriate confidentiality, cybersecurity, insider-risk, and intellectual-property protection, use, and nondisclosure requirements, for a period of up to 30 days before they plan to release such models to other trusted partners; and 

 (iii)  collaborate with the Federal Government to select trusted partners that will have early access to covered frontier models to promote secure innovation and strengthen the cybersecurity of critical infrastructure.

 (c)  Nothing in this section shall be construed to authorize the creation of a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for the development, publication, release, or distribution of new AI models, including frontier models.

 Sec . 4 .   Protection Against Criminal Actors .  The Attorney General shall prioritize the enforcement of 18 U.S.C. 1028, 18 U.S.C. 1030, 18 U.S.C. 1343, and all other applicable Federal criminal laws against anyone who utilizes AI

I can cite EO 14409 Sec. 3.
- Sunset: "This section shall terminate on the date that is 3 years after the date of the enactment of this section" — that appears to be Sec. 102(i)? The snippet shows "(i) SUNSET.—This section shall terminate on the date that is 3 years after the date of the enactment of this section." right before Sec. 111. So Sec. 102 (CAISI section?) — hmm, actually it appears right before "Subtitle B—Transparency, Independent Verification, and Whistleblower Protections SEC. 111..." — so the "(i) SUNSET" is the last subsection of Sec. 102? Actually wait. Let me reconsider. DLA Piper said "Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years." Q1 (Majority E&C staff): "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."
Answer: We don't oppose incident reporting as such; we oppose the definition as drafted. Sec. 101(7) makes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" or "loss of control" a reportable incident with no demonstrated harm required. That's broader than SB 53's harm-based trigger. Speculative triggers convert the reporting duty into a paperwork engine and drown CAISI in noise. Q2 (Minority, Trahan-aligned): "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"
Answer: A short list we support: published frontier AI frameworks for large frontier developers (Sec. 111(a)); transparency reports at deployment (Sec. 111(c)); 15-day critical safety incident reporting keyed to demonstrated harm; whistleblower anti-retaliation protections (Sec. 113); GAO review of model-weight security (Sec. 321); CAISI's voluntary standards work (Sec. 102). Q3 (Senate Commerce staff): "Three years or permanent — what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed in July, phases in next year. Three statutes, three sets of definitions, three reporting clocks and three enforcement regimes, aimed at the same handful of national developers. And more coming.

Survey data: 61% cite conflicting state definitions as top compliance issue; 34% of startup members delayed launch in CA/NY; median 6.5 FTEs for parallel SB 53 + RAISE compliance; $310k one-off incident-reporting stand-up; $1.4M median annual framework maintenance for developers above $500M revenue. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, which don't have compliance departments; the patchwork advantages the largest incumbents, who can absorb 50 sets of rules and often help write them.

We endorse the finding in Sec. 121 that development of AI models is "a matter of national economic significance and international competitiveness requiring uniform Federal oversight." One national standard, not fifty discordant ones. This also aligns with the administration's framework (Dec 2025 EO; Mar 20, 2026 White House framework urging preemption of "undue burdens").

**II. Preemption: support; make it durable (Sec. 121)**
Support the development-focused scope: it is where the conflicts are sharpest and where a national market must be preserved; states remain free to regulate use and deployment, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies unaffected.
But: the three-year clock creates a cliff. Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment; the federalization provision lapses in the same window unless reauthorized. In year three, the federal standard disappears and the states return, likely with more aggressive regimes, while our members are mid-buildout on capital plans that run five to ten years. Ask: make Sec. 121 permanent; at minimum, extend it and reauthorize the federal standard well before any sunset so that no gap ever opens.

**III. Critical safety incident reporting: oppose as drafted (Secs. 101(7), 111(f)-(g), 111(i))**
ACIA does not oppose incident reporting in principle. Our members run the disclosure and escalation processes already required by SB 53 and soon by RAISE. What we cannot support is the definition as drafted.
Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control," with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed. Under that definition, a safeguard that performs below expectations, or an unproven hypothesis about hypothetical model behavior, becomes a federal reportable event. Catastrophic-risk scenarios of this kind are speculative, and speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. The bill should regulate demonstrated harms. Requested changes:
1. Narrow Sec. 101(7): a reportable incident should require demonstrated harm: actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage, or actual compromise of critical infrastructure, arising from a frontier model. Keep unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights as a concrete, reportable event, but tie the failure and loss-of-control prongs to real-world outcomes, not scenario analysis.
2. Preserve the 15-day window (Sec. 111(g)) and the 24-hour imminent-danger channel. These mirror SB 53. Resist pressure to conform to New York's 72-hour clock: shorter clocks don't produce better information, they produce more noise and more lawyer-driven over-reporting, which is exactly what CAISI's nascent reporting function does not need.
3. Extend the draft's own confidentiality protections to incident reports. Sec. 102 already exempts information shared with the Center from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) and bars its reuse by other regulators. Incident reports, which will necessarily contain security-sensitive details, deserve the same explicit exemption. (Confirm the reporting subsection inherits Sec. 102 protections; if not, add parallel language to Sec. 111.)
4. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reports. Sec. 111(i) authorizes civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each continuing day a separate violation. Under that exposure, honest reporting of a marginal event invites enforcement; silence becomes rational. A good-faith reporter should not face penalties based on the contents of its own report. Tier penalties for non-willful procedural violations and require notice-and-cure first.

**IV. Verification and audits: restructure (Sec. 112)** 
The IVO regime is the heaviest single provision. It requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed auditors, give them access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with mandatory referrals to federal and state AGs where the IVO sees "imminent catastrophic risk." Semi-annual is heavier than any of the state statutes it would replace (annual in each). And the IVO's mandate is keyed not to compliance but to whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation": an open-ended invitation to second-guess engineering judgment on speculative scenarios. Requests: annual, verification-focused audits; confidentiality for audit materials; ad hoc audits only on articulable facts, not hypotheticals; mandatory referrals tied to imminent, demonstrated harm.

**V. CAISI: support a voluntary mission (Sec. 102)**
Support codification and $100M-scale capacity for voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring; this mirrors the House AI Task Force recommendations and the administration's approach: EO 14409's Sec. 3 voluntary pre-release engagement expressly disclaims any mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance or permitting requirement. Two requests: (1) keep the evaluation function voluntary, collaborative and confidential, with the EO 14409 no-gate language written into statute; (2) as the draft moves to introduction, we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI or any release gate. The center's value is credibility and technical expertise, not veto power. No position on the authorization level; we note the fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers passes costs through to industry.

**VI. Provisions we support without reservation**
- Sec. 111(a), (c): framework + transparency reports, redaction authority. Members above the $500M threshold spend median $1.4M/yr to maintain published frameworks; disclosure at that scale is workable, and the revenue floors at Sec. 101 keep the heaviest duties off pre-revenue startups. Keep the redaction authority for trade secrets, cybersecurity and national security intact.
- Sec. 113 whistleblower anti-retaliation: support; ask only that "AI violation" be defined by reference to violations of this Act, not any federal statute touching AI, so the provision doesn't become a roving federal cause of action.
- Secs. 401 testbeds, 423 NAIRR, 411 international standards coalitions excluding China, 311 CISA open-source grants, 321 GAO model-weight security review, 132 impersonation penalties. Support.

**VII. Costs** — recap; compliance costs fall hardest on startups; the fix is one national standard, light-touch, risk-based, keyed to demonstrated harms.

**VIII. Conclusion** — offer technical assistance; contact VP Policy Tessa Marchetti; thank.

Respectfully,
Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Comment letter

[ACIA LETTERHEAD]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: ACIA comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for the open process you have run since releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 on June 4, and for the bipartisan example you have set with Reps. Franklin, Subramanyam, Houchin and Peters. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of roughly 140 members: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, silicon and compute infrastructure on which American AI leadership depends. We write to endorse the draft's central architecture and to request specific changes before introduction.

Our positions in brief. We strongly support the federalization provision in Sec. 121 and ask that it be made permanent, or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before any sunset. We oppose the critical safety incident provisions as drafted, Secs. 101(7) and 111(f)-(g), for four fixable reasons. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) with a voluntary standards mission under Sec. 102, and we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority added as the bill moves. We take no position on the $100 million annual authorization.

I. The patchwork is not a hypothetical. It is a line item.

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect January 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by the chapter amendment signed March 27, takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, phases in next year. Three frontier-AI statutes in three states inside eighteen months, each with its own definitions, reporting clocks, audit expectations and enforcement apparatus, aimed at the same handful of nationally operating developers. Nearly every week brings another state proposal.

Our members are living with the results. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of our startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past twelve months because of state AI rules. The developers among our members that must comply with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on dual compliance. Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median of $310,000 before the first report is ever filed, and members above the draft's $500 million revenue threshold spend a median of $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

These costs are not evenly shared. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, which do not have compliance departments. The largest incumbents can absorb fifty state regimes and, frankly, benefit from the moat. That is why ACIA's members, competitors in most things, are united on this: one clear federal standard, light-touch and risk-based, beats a fifty-state patchwork.

We endorse the finding in Sec. 121 that the development of AI models is "a matter of national economic significance and international competitiveness requiring uniform Federal oversight." The direction is also consistent with the executive branch's own posture: the December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20 legislative framework asked Congress to preempt state laws that impose "undue burdens" in favor of "a minimally burdensome national standard." Your draft is the vehicle.

II. Preemption: make the standard durable

The draft's federalization provision is well scoped. It reaches state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models, where the conflicts are sharpest, and leaves states their traditional authority over deployment, use and laws of general applicability, along with common-law remedies. That balance is right, and we support it.

Our concern is the clock. The obligations in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment, and the federalization provision lapses in the same window unless reauthorized. Year three is therefore the worst possible outcome: the federal standard disappears, the states return, and companies that spent three years building to a federal specification start over. Compute and data-center investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is not a standard; it is a countdown.

Requested change: make Sec. 121 permanent. If permanence is not achievable in this Congress, extend the provision and require reauthorization of the federal standard well before any sunset, so that at no point does the country revert to the patchwork the draft was written to end.

III. Incident reporting: oppose as drafted, with four fixes

ACIA does not oppose incident reporting in principle. Our members already run disclosure and escalation processes under SB 53 and are preparing for RAISE. What we cannot support is the draft's definition of what must be reported.

Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a frontier model, with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed. Under that definition, a mitigation that underperforms an internal threshold, or a hypothesis about hypothetical model behavior, becomes a federal reportable event. Catastrophic-risk scenarios of this kind are speculative, and speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. A federal reporting regime should be keyed to demonstrated harms.

We ask for four changes:

1. Narrow the definition. A reportable incident under Sec. 101(7) should require demonstrated harm: actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage, or actual compromise of critical infrastructure, arising from a frontier model. Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights is a concrete security event and is appropriately reportable. The failure and loss-of-control prongs, as drafted, would import scenario analysis into a regulatory filing.

2. Preserve the 15-day window. The draft's 15-day reporting clock and its 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury mirror SB 53, and we support them. Resist any pressure to conform to New York's 72-hour clock, and note that separate proposals in Congress would set clocks as short as seven days. Shorter windows do not produce better information. They produce hurried, lawyer-driven over-reporting that buries the regulator in noise and, with it, the genuinely serious incidents the regime exists to catch.

3. Extend the draft's own confidentiality protections to incident reports. Sec. 102 already exempts information shared with the Center from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) and bars its reuse by other regulators. Incident reports will necessarily describe security-sensitive details, including vulnerabilities; publishing or leaking them would create the very risks the provision is meant to prevent. Please confirm the reporting subsection inherits those protections, and if it does not, add parallel language to Sec. 111.

4. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reports. Sec. 111(i) sets penalties at up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately. At that exposure, an honest report of a marginal event hands the government its case, and silence becomes the rational strategy. That is backwards. A good-faith report should not be used as evidence of a violation, and penalties for non-willful, procedural violations should be tiered and preceded by notice and an opportunity to cure.

IV. Verification and audits: restructure Sec. 112

The independent verification organization (IVO) regime is the heaviest single provision in the draft. Large frontier developers must retain CAISI-licensed auditors, grant them timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with mandatory referral to federal and state attorneys general where an IVO perceives "imminent catastrophic risk."

Two problems. Semi-annual audits are heavier than any state regime the draft would replace; New York and Illinois each settled on annual review cycles. And the IVO's mandate is keyed not to compliance but to whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," an open-ended invitation to second-guess engineering judgment against speculative scenarios.

Requested changes: align the audit cadence to annual; scope audits to verification of the developer's compliance with its published framework and with the Act; protect audit materials with the same confidentiality as Sec. 102 information; limit ad hoc audits to articulable facts rather than hypotheticals; and tie mandatory referrals to imminent, demonstrated harm.

V. CAISI: a voluntary mission

We support codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce, Sec. 102, and the substantial capacity the draft would give it for voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring. This builds on the House AI Task Force's recommendations and mirrors the administration's approach: Executive Order 14409 establishes voluntary pre-release engagement with covered frontier models and expressly disclaims any mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance or permitting requirement for new models.

Two requests. First, keep CAISI's evaluation work voluntary, collaborative and confidential, and write EO 14409's no-gate language into the statute. Second, we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI or any release gate added as the draft moves. The center's value to the industry and to the government is technical credibility, not veto power. On the $100 million annual authorization we take no position; we note only that the draft's fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers passes costs through to the regulated.

VI. Provisions we support

Sec. 111(a) and (c): published frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports, with the revenue floors in Sec. 101 and the redaction authority for trade secrets, cybersecurity and national security intact. Disclosure at the scale of the largest developers is workable; our members above the threshold already do it, at a median of $1.4 million a year.

Sec. 113: whistleblower anti-retaliation protections. We support them. One clarification: "AI violation" should be defined by reference to violations of this Act, not of any federal statute touching AI, so the provision does not become a roving federal cause of action.

Secs. 401, 411, 423, 311, 321 and 132: the AI testbed program at DOE and NIST with NSF; international standards coalitions that exclude China; codification of the National AI Research Resource; CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; the GAO review of model-weight and data-center security; and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support all of them. They invest in the innovation side of the ledger, which is where America wins.

VII. Conclusion

The Great American AI Act asks the right question: whether the United States will govern frontier AI under one national standard or fifty discordant ones. ACIA's answer is the same as our March 2025 comment to OSTP: preempt the patchwork. As drafted, the bill would do that, but on a clock too short to bank investment against, and with a reporting definition that treats speculative scenarios as reportable events.

One national standard, light-touch and risk-based, keyed to demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones, and durable enough to plan against. Our members would support that bill enthusiastically, and we stand ready to help you write it.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Questions and technical assistance requests may be directed to Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
