---

[ACIA letterhead]
October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: ACIA comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, released June 4. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture investors. Our members build the models, the silicon and the compute infrastructure that will determine whether the United States leads this decade. We write both to endorse the draft's central architecture and to request specific fixes before introduction.

**Summary position** (short). ACIA supports the draft's federalization provision. We oppose the critical safety incident reporting provision as drafted. We support codifying CAISI with a voluntary standards mission, and we would oppose any move to give it mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. Details and requested changes below.

**I. The patchwork is not a hypothetical** — costs. 

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect January 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March, takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed in July, phases in next year. Three statutes, three sets of definitions, three reporting clocks and three enforcement regimes, aimed at the same handful of national developers. And more coming.

Survey data: 61% cite conflicting state definitions as top compliance issue; 34% of startup members delayed launch in CA/NY; median 6.5 FTEs for parallel SB 53 + RAISE compliance; $310k one-off incident-reporting stand-up; $1.4M median annual framework maintenance for developers above $500M revenue. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, which don't have compliance departments; the patchwork advantages the largest incumbents, who can absorb 50 sets of rules and often help write them.

We endorse the finding in Sec. 121 that development of AI models is "a matter of national economic significance and international competitiveness requiring uniform Federal oversight." One national standard, not fifty discordant ones. This also aligns with the administration's framework (Dec 2025 EO; Mar 20, 2026 White House framework urging preemption of "undue burdens").

**II. Preemption: support; make it durable (Sec. 121)**
Support the development-focused scope: it is where the conflicts are sharpest and where a national market must be preserved; states remain free to regulate use and deployment, general-applicability laws and common-law remedies unaffected.
But: the three-year clock creates a cliff. Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment; the federalization provision lapses in the same window unless reauthorized. In year three, the federal standard disappears and the states return, likely with more aggressive regimes, while our members are mid-buildout on capital plans that run five to ten years. Ask: make Sec. 121 permanent; at minimum, extend it and reauthorize the federal standard well before any sunset so that no gap ever opens.

**III. Critical safety incident reporting: oppose as drafted (Secs. 101(7), 111(f)-(g), 111(i))**
ACIA does not oppose incident reporting in principle. Our members run the disclosure and escalation processes already required by SB 53 and soon by RAISE. What we cannot support is the definition as drafted.
Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control," with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed. Under that definition, a safeguard that performs below expectations, or an unproven hypothesis about hypothetical model behavior, becomes a federal reportable event. Catastrophic-risk scenarios of this kind are speculative, and speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. The bill should regulate demonstrated harms. Requested changes:
1. Narrow Sec. 101(7): a reportable incident should require demonstrated harm: actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage, or actual compromise of critical infrastructure, arising from a frontier model. Keep unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights as a concrete, reportable event, but tie the failure and loss-of-control prongs to real-world outcomes, not scenario analysis.
2. Preserve the 15-day window (Sec. 111(g)) and the 24-hour imminent-danger channel. These mirror SB 53. Resist pressure to conform to New York's 72-hour clock: shorter clocks don't produce better information, they produce more noise and more lawyer-driven over-reporting, which is exactly what CAISI's nascent reporting function does not need.
3. Extend the draft's own confidentiality protections to incident reports. Sec. 102 already exempts information shared with the Center from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) and bars its reuse by other regulators. Incident reports, which will necessarily contain security-sensitive details, deserve the same explicit exemption. (Confirm the reporting subsection inherits Sec. 102 protections; if not, add parallel language to Sec. 111.)
4. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reports. Sec. 111(i) authorizes civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each continuing day a separate violation. Under that exposure, honest reporting of a marginal event invites enforcement; silence becomes rational. A good-faith reporter should not face penalties based on the contents of its own report. Tier penalties for non-willful procedural violations and require notice-and-cure first.

**IV. Verification and audits: restructure (Sec. 112)** 
The IVO regime is the heaviest single provision. It requires large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed auditors, give them access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with mandatory referrals to federal and state AGs where the IVO sees "imminent catastrophic risk." And the IVO's mandate is keyed not to compliance but to whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation": an open-ended invitation to second-guess engineering judgment on speculative scenarios. Two requests: (1) keep the evaluation function voluntary, collaborative and confidential, with the EO 14409 no-gate language written into statute; (2) as the draft moves to introduction, we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI or any release gate. The center's value is credibility and technical expertise, not veto power. No position on the authorization level; we note the fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers passes costs through to industry.

**VI. Provisions we support without reservation**
- Sec. 111(a), (c): framework + transparency reports, redaction authority. Members above the $500M threshold spend median $1.4M/yr to maintain published frameworks; disclosure at that scale is workable, and the revenue floors at Sec. 101 keep the heaviest duties off pre-revenue startups. Keep the redaction authority for trade secrets, cybersecurity and national security intact.

**VII. Costs** — recap; compliance costs fall hardest on startups; the fix is one national standard, light-touch, risk-based, keyed to demonstrated harms.

**VIII. Conclusion** — offer technical assistance; contact VP Policy Tessa Marchetti; thank.

Respectfully,

President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Comment letter

[ACIA LETTERHEAD]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: ACIA comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for the open process you have run since releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 on June 4, and for the bipartisan example you have set with Reps. Franklin, Subramanyam, Houchin and Peters. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of roughly 140 members: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, silicon and compute infrastructure on which American AI leadership depends. We write to endorse the draft's central architecture and to request specific changes before introduction.

Our positions in brief. We strongly support the federalization provision in Sec. 121 and ask that it be made permanent, or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before any sunset. We oppose the critical safety incident provisions as drafted, Secs. 101(7) and 111(f)-(g), for four fixable reasons. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) with a voluntary standards mission under Sec. 102, and we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority added as the bill moves. We take no position on the $100 million annual authorization.

I. The patchwork is not a hypothetical. It is a line item.

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect January 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended by the chapter amendment signed March 27, takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, phases in next year. Three frontier-AI statutes in three states inside eighteen months, each with its own definitions, reporting clocks, audit expectations and enforcement apparatus, aimed at the same handful of nationally operating developers. Nearly every week brings another state proposal.

Our members are living with the results. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of our startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past twelve months because of state AI rules. The developers among our members that must comply with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on dual compliance. Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median of $310,000 before the first report is ever filed, and members above the draft's $500 million revenue threshold spend a median of $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

These costs are not evenly shared. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, which do not have compliance departments. The largest incumbents can absorb fifty state regimes and, frankly, benefit from the moat. That is why ACIA's members, competitors in most things, are united on this: one clear federal standard, light-touch and risk-based, beats a fifty-state patchwork.

We endorse the finding in Sec. 121 that the development of AI models is "a matter of national economic significance and international competitiveness requiring uniform Federal oversight." The direction is also consistent with the executive branch's own posture: the December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20 legislative framework asked Congress to preempt state laws that impose "undue burdens" in favor of "a minimally burdensome national standard." Your draft is the vehicle.

II. Preemption: make the standard durable

The draft's federalization provision is well scoped. It reaches state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models, where the conflicts are sharpest, and leaves states their traditional authority over deployment, use and laws of general applicability, along with common-law remedies. That balance is right, and we support it.

Our concern is the clock. The obligations in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment, and the federalization provision lapses in the same window unless reauthorized. Year three is therefore the worst possible outcome: the federal standard disappears, the states return, and companies that spent three years building to a federal specification start over. Compute and data-center investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is not a standard; it is a countdown.

Requested change: make Sec. 121 permanent. If permanence is not achievable in this Congress, extend the provision and require reauthorization of the federal standard well before any sunset, so that at no point does the country revert to the patchwork the draft was written to end.

III. Incident reporting: oppose as drafted, with four fixes

ACIA does not oppose incident reporting in principle. Our members already run disclosure and escalation processes under SB 53 and are preparing for RAISE. What we cannot support is the draft's definition of what must be reported.

Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a frontier model, with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed. Under that definition, a mitigation that underperforms an internal threshold, or a hypothesis about hypothetical model behavior, becomes a federal reportable event. Catastrophic-risk scenarios of this kind are speculative, and speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. A federal reporting regime should be keyed to demonstrated harms.

We ask for four changes:

1. Narrow the definition. A reportable incident under Sec. 101(7) should require demonstrated harm: actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage, or actual compromise of critical infrastructure, arising from a frontier model. Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights is a concrete security event and is appropriately reportable. The failure and loss-of-control prongs, as drafted, would import scenario analysis into a regulatory filing.

2. Preserve the 15-day window. The draft's 15-day reporting clock and its 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury mirror SB 53, and we support them. Resist any pressure to conform to New York's 72-hour clock, and note that separate proposals in Congress would set clocks as short as seven days. Shorter windows do not produce better information. They produce hurried, lawyer-driven over-reporting that buries the regulator in noise and, with it, the genuinely serious incidents the regime exists to catch.

3. Extend the draft's own confidentiality protections to incident reports. Sec. 102 already exempts information shared with the Center from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) and bars its reuse by other regulators. Incident reports will necessarily describe security-sensitive details, including vulnerabilities; publishing or leaking them would create the very risks the provision is meant to prevent. Please confirm the reporting subsection inherits those protections, and if it does not, add parallel language to Sec. 111.

4. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reports. Sec. 111(i) sets penalties at up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately. At that exposure, an honest report of a marginal event hands the government its case, and silence becomes the rational strategy. That is backwards. A good-faith report should not be used as evidence of a violation, and penalties for non-willful, procedural violations should be tiered and preceded by notice and an opportunity to cure.

IV. Verification and audits: restructure Sec. 112

The independent verification organization (IVO) regime is the heaviest single provision in the draft. Large frontier developers must retain CAISI-licensed auditors, grant them timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with mandatory referral to federal and state attorneys general where an IVO perceives "imminent catastrophic risk."

Two problems. Semi-annual audits are heavier than any state regime the draft would replace; New York and Illinois each settled on annual review cycles. And the IVO's mandate is keyed not to compliance but to whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," an open-ended invitation to second-guess engineering judgment against speculative scenarios.

Requested changes: align the audit cadence to annual; scope audits to verification of the developer's compliance with its published framework and with the Act; protect audit materials with the same confidentiality as Sec. 102 information; limit ad hoc audits to articulable facts rather than hypotheticals; and tie mandatory referrals to imminent, demonstrated harm.

V. CAISI: a voluntary mission

We support codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce, Sec. 102, and the substantial capacity the draft would give it for voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring. This builds on the House AI Task Force's recommendations and mirrors the administration's approach: Executive Order 14409 establishes voluntary pre-release engagement with covered frontier models and expressly disclaims any mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance or permitting requirement for new models.

Two requests. First, keep CAISI's evaluation work voluntary, collaborative and confidential, and write EO 14409's no-gate language into the statute. Second, we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI or any release gate added as the draft moves. The center's value to the industry and to the government is technical credibility, not veto power. On the $100 million annual authorization we take no position; we note only that the draft's fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers passes costs through to the regulated.

VI. Provisions we support

Sec. 111(a) and (c): published frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports, with the revenue floors in Sec. 101 and the redaction authority for trade secrets, cybersecurity and national security intact. Disclosure at the scale of the largest developers is workable; our members above the threshold already do it, at a median of $1.4 million a year.

Sec. 113: whistleblower anti-retaliation protections. We support them. One clarification: "AI violation" should be defined by reference to violations of this Act, not of any federal statute touching AI, so the provision does not become a roving federal cause of action.

Secs. 401, 411, 423, 311, 321 and 132: the AI testbed program at DOE and NIST with NSF; international standards coalitions that exclude China; codification of the National AI Research Resource; CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; the GAO review of model-weight and data-center security; and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support all of them. They invest in the innovation side of the ledger, which is where America wins.

VII. Conclusion

The Great American AI Act asks the right question: whether the United States will govern frontier AI under one national standard or fifty discordant ones. ACIA's answer is the same as our March 2025 comment to OSTP: preempt the patchwork. As drafted, the bill would do that, but on a clock too short to bank investment against, and with a reporting definition that treats speculative scenarios as reportable events.

One national standard, light-touch and risk-based, keyed to demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones, and durable enough to plan against. Our members would support that bill enthusiastically, and we stand ready to help you write it.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Questions and technical assistance requests may be directed to Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

{"content":"# ACIA Comment Letter: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act Discussion Draft

**DRAFT for President & CEO sign-off (ACIA-POL-2026-117). Not sent. To be transmitted to GAAIA@mail.house.gov.**

---

[ACIA LETTERHEAD]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: ACIA comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for the open process you have run since releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act on June 4, and for the bipartisan example you have set with Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of roughly 140 members: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the silicon and the compute infrastructure on which American AI leadership depends. We write to endorse the draft's central architecture and to request specific changes before introduction.

Our positions in brief. We strongly support the federalization provision in Sec. 121 and ask that it be made permanent, or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before any sunset. We oppose the critical safety incident provisions as drafted, Secs. 101(7) and 111(f)-(g), for four fixable reasons. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) with a voluntary standards mission under Sec. 102, and we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority added as the bill moves. We take no position on the $100 million annual authorization.

## I. The patchwork is not a hypothetical. It is a line item.

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect January 1. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by the chapter amendment signed March 27, takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, phases in through 2028. Three frontier-AI statutes in three states inside eighteen months, each with its own definitions, reporting clocks, audit expectations and enforcement apparatus, aimed at the same handful of nationally operating developers.

Our members are living with the results. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of our startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past twelve months because of state AI rules. Our developer members that must comply with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on dual compliance. Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median of $310,000 before the first report is ever filed, and our developer members above the draft's $500 million revenue threshold spend a median of $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

These costs are not evenly shared. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, which do not have compliance departments. The largest incumbents can absorb fifty state regimes and, candidly, benefit from the moat. That is why ACIA's members, competitors in nearly everything, are united on this: one clear federal standard, light-touch and risk-based, beats a fifty-state patchwork.

We endorse the finding in Sec. 121 that the development of AI models is "a matter of national economic significance and international competitiveness requiring uniform Federal oversight." The direction matches the executive branch's own posture. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20 legislative framework asked Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose "undue burdens" in favor of "a minimally burdensome national standard." Your draft is the vehicle.

## II. Preemption: make the standard durable

The draft's federalization provision is well scoped. It reaches state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models, where the conflicts are sharpest, and leaves states their traditional authority over deployment, use and laws of general applicability, along with common-law remedies. That balance is right. We support it.

Our concern is the clock. The obligations in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment, and the federalization provision lapses in the same window unless reauthorized. Year three is therefore the worst possible outcome: the federal standard disappears, the states return, and companies that spent three years building to a federal specification start over. Compute and data-center investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is not a standard. It is a countdown.

Requested change: make Sec. 121 permanent. If permanence is not achievable in this Congress, extend the provision and require reauthorization of the federal standard well before any sunset, so that at no point does the country revert to the patchwork the draft was written to end.

## III. Incident reporting: oppose as drafted, with four fixes

ACIA does not oppose incident reporting in principle. Our members already run disclosure and escalation processes under SB 53 and are preparing for RAISE. What we cannot support is the draft's definition of what must be reported.

Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a frontier model, with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed. Under that definition, a mitigation that underperforms an internal threshold becomes a federal reportable event. Catastrophic-risk scenarios of this kind are speculative, and speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. A federal reporting regime should be keyed to demonstrated harms.

We ask for four changes.

1. **Narrow the definition.** A reportable incident under Sec. 101(7) should require demonstrated harm: actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage, or actual compromise of critical infrastructure, arising from a frontier model. Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights is a concrete security event and is appropriately reportable. The failure and loss-of-control prongs, as drafted, would import scenario analysis into a regulatory filing.

2. **Preserve the 15-day window.** The draft's 15-day reporting clock and its 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury mirror SB 53, and we support them. Resist any pressure to conform to New York's 72-hour clock, and note that separate proposals in Congress would set clocks as short as seven days. Shorter windows do not produce better information. They produce hurried, lawyer-driven over-reporting that buries the regulator in noise, and with it the genuinely serious incidents the regime exists to catch.

3. **Extend the draft's own confidentiality protections to incident reports.** Sec. 102 already exempts information shared with the Center from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) and bars its reuse by other regulators. Incident reports will necessarily describe security-sensitive details, including vulnerabilities. Publishing or leaking them would create the very risks the provision is meant to prevent. Please confirm the reporting subsection inherits those protections, and if it does not, add parallel language to Sec. 111.

4. **Add a safe harbor for good-faith reports.** Sec. 111(i) sets penalties at up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately. At that exposure, an honest report of a marginal event hands the government its case, and silence becomes the rational strategy. That is backwards. A good-faith report should not be usable as evidence of a violation, and penalties for non-willful, procedural violations should be tiered and preceded by notice and an opportunity to cure.

## IV. Verification and audits: restructure Sec. 112

The independent verification organization (IVO) regime is the heaviest single provision in the draft. Large frontier developers must retain CAISI-licensed auditors, grant them timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with mandatory referral to federal and state attorneys general where an IVO perceives "imminent catastrophic risk."

Two problems. Semi-annual audits are heavier than any state regime the draft would replace; New York and Illinois each settled on annual review cycles. And the IVO's mandate is keyed not to compliance but to whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," an open-ended invitation to second-guess engineering judgment against speculative scenarios.

Requested changes: align the audit cadence to annual; scope audits to verification of the developer's compliance with its published framework and with the Act; protect audit materials with the same confidentiality as Sec. 102 information; limit ad hoc audits to articulable facts rather than hypotheticals; and tie mandatory referrals to imminent, demonstrated harm.

## V. CAISI: a voluntary mission

We support codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce under Sec. 102, with the substantial capacity the draft would give it for voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring. This builds on recommendations of the House AI Task Force and mirrors the administration's approach. Executive Order 14409 of June 2 establishes voluntary pre-release engagement with covered frontier models and expressly disclaims any "mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement" for new models.

Two requests. First, keep CAISI's evaluation work voluntary, collaborative and confidential, and write EO 14409's no-gate language into the statute. Second, we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, or any release gate, added as the draft moves. The center's value to industry and government is technical credibility, not veto power. On the $100 million annual authorization we take no position. We note only that the draft's fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers passes costs through to the regulated.

## VI. Provisions we support

**Sec. 111(a) and (c):** published frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports, with the revenue floors in Sec. 101 and the redaction authority for trade secrets, cybersecurity and national security intact. Disclosure at the scale of the largest developers is workable; our members above the threshold already do it, at a median of $1.4 million a year.

**Sec. 113:** whistleblower anti-retaliation protections, which we support. One clarification: "AI violation" should be defined by reference to violations of this Act, not of any federal statute touching AI, so the provision does not become a roving federal cause of action.

**Secs. 401, 411, 423, 311, 321 and 132:** the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST; international standards coalitions that exclude China; codification of the National AI Research Resource; CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; the GAO review of model-weight and data-center security; and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support all of them. They invest in the innovation side of the ledger, which is where America wins.

## VII. Conclusion

The Great American AI Act asks the right question: whether the United States will govern frontier AI under one national standard or fifty discordant ones. ACIA's answer is the same one we gave OSTP in our March 2025 comment on the AI Action Plan: preempt the patchwork. As drafted, the bill would do that, but on a clock too short to bank investment against, and with a reporting definition that treats speculative scenarios as reportable events.

Our members would support enthusiastically a bill that does the following: one national standard, light-touch and risk-based, keyed to demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones, and durable enough to plan against. We stand ready to help you write it.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Questions and offers of technical assistance may be directed to Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President and CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

**ACIA on the Great American AI Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan), House Energy & Commerce**

**Bottom line.** ACIA, a coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms, supports the draft's core: one national standard for AI model development instead of a fifty-state patchwork. With five targeted fixes, our members will support it enthusiastically.

**Why it matters.** Three frontier-AI statutes landed in eighteen months: California SB 53 (in effect Jan. 1, 2026), New York's RAISE Act (effective Jan. 1, 2027) and Illinois SB 315 (signed July 2026). Each carries its own definitions, clocks and enforcement. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members), 61% named conflicting state definitions their top compliance problem, 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York last year, and developers complying with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 full-time employees. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. The patchwork is a moat around the largest incumbents.

## ACIA's five asks

**1. Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** The development-focused scope is right and we support it. But Secs. 111 and 112 sunset, and preemption lapses, in the same three-year window, so in year three the federal standard disappears and states return mid-buildout. Compute investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is a countdown, not a standard. At minimum, extend preemption with the federal standard reauthorized and in place before any sunset.

**2. Define "critical safety incident" by demonstrated harm (Sec. 101(7)).** As drafted, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" or "loss of control" is reportable with no one harmed. Speculative catastrophic-risk scenarios are not a sound basis for legislation. Require actual death, serious injury, major property damage or actual critical-infrastructure compromise.

**3. Keep the 15-day reporting window (Sec. 111(f)-(g)).** The draft matches SB 53's 15 days plus a 24-hour imminent-danger channel. Do not follow New York's 72-hour clock or the seven-day proposals floating in Congress. Short clocks produce noise, not information.

**4. Protect good-faith reporters (Secs. 111(g), (i)).** Extend the draft's own FOIA exemption (5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), as in Sec. 102) to incident reports, and add a safe harbor so an honest report cannot be used as evidence of a violation. Penalties now reach $1 million per violation, per day.

**5. Keep CAISI voluntary and right-size audits (Secs. 102, 112).** Support codification and the voluntary standards mission; oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority or release gate, consistent with EO 14409's express no-gate language. Move IVO audits to an annual, compliance-focused cadence; semi-annual is heavier than any state law it would replace.

**Also support:** NAIRR codification, AI testbeds, international standards coalitions excluding China, CISA open-source security grants and the GAO model-weight security review.

**Contact:** Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.

Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117. Section numbers are to the June 4, 2026, discussion draft; re-verify against introduced text before external use. Positions per ACIA Messaging Guide v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026).

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 121.** Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development (3 years unless reauthorized) | SUPPORT | Make permanent; at minimum extend, with the federal standard reauthorized and in place before any sunset | One national standard beats a fifty-state patchwork, and a three-year countdown to the patchwork's return is a cliff, not a framework. |
| **Sec. 101(7).** "Critical safety incident" definition (weight theft; failure of risk-mitigation measures; loss of control) | OPPOSE AS DRAFTED | Require demonstrated harm (actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage, actual critical-infrastructure compromise); keep model-weight theft reportable as a concrete security event | Speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation; reporting should turn on demonstrated harms, not hypotheses. |
| **Sec. 111(f)-(g).** Critical safety incident reports to CAISI Director; 15 days; 24 hours if imminent risk of death or serious physical injury | OPPOSE AS DRAFTED (fixable) | Keep the 15-day window; reject any move to RAISE's 72-hour clock or shorter proposals (a 7-day bill has been introduced separately); add confidentiality/FOIA exemption mirroring Sec. 102's 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) protection; add a good-faith safe harbor | Short clocks and speculative triggers generate noise, and unprotected, penalized reporting punishes candor. |
| **Sec. 111(a), (c).** Published frontier AI frameworks (large frontier developers) and transparency reports (frontier developers), with redaction authority | SUPPORT | None, except preserve the redaction authority and the Sec. 101 revenue floors ($50M/$500M) so the heaviest duties stay off startups | Light-touch disclosure our largest members already practice; compliance costs fall hardest on startups. |
| **Sec. 111(i).** Civil penalties up to $1M per violation, each continuing day a separate violation; AG and opt-in state AG enforcement | CONCERN | Tier penalties for non-willful procedural violations; notice and cure before penalties; safe harbor for good-faith reports | Enforcement should be light-touch and risk-based, not a per-day meter on paperwork lapses. |
| **Sec. 112.** CAISI-licensed IVO audits of large frontier developers; semi-annual plus ad hoc at Director's request; access to unredacted materials; mandatory referral on "imminent catastrophic risk" | OPPOSE AS DRAFTED | Annual, compliance-verification audits; confidentiality for audit materials; ad hoc audits only on articulable facts; mandatory referrals tied to imminent, demonstrated harm | Semi-annual is heavier than any state regime it replaces, and auditing against "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" second-guesses engineering judgment on speculative scenarios. |
| **Sec. 102.** CAISI codified at Commerce; voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation and monitoring; IVO licensing; $100M/yr authorized FY2027-2029; fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers | SUPPORT (voluntary role); NO POSITION on funding level | Keep evaluation work voluntary, collaborative, confidential; write EO 14409's no-gate language into statute; oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority or release gate; scrutinize fee pass-throughs | CAISI's value is technical credibility as a standards partner, not veto power. |
| **Sec. 113.** Whistleblower anti-retaliation protections ("AI violation" = any violation of federal law related to AI development, deployment or operation) | SUPPORT WITH CLARIFICATION | Define "AI violation" by reference to violations of this Act | A roving cause of action spanning all federal AI law invites abusive litigation. |
| **Sec. 122 / Sec. 321.** GAO review of federal AI adoption; GAO report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security | SUPPORT | None; fund and schedule them | Oversight of demonstrated problems without new mandates. |
| **Sec. 311.** CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; large frontier developers provide model access to maintainers | SUPPORT | Ensure access obligations are workable and IP-safe | Hardening the open-source base is security, not regulation. |
| **Sec. 401 / Sec. 411 / Sec. 423.** AI testbeds (DOE, NIST, NSF); international standards coalitions excluding China; NAIRR codification | SUPPORT | Appropriate robustly | America wins the AI race on innovation and compute buildout; these provisions invest in it. |
| **Sec. 132.** Penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials | SUPPORT | None | Targets a concrete, demonstrated harm. |

## Cost context (ACIA member survey, Aug 2026; aggregate only, never name a member)

- 61% of members cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue.
- 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months.
- Median 6.5 FTEs (IQR 4-11, n=11) to comply with SB 53 plus RAISE in parallel.

- Median $1.4 million annual cost (IQR $0.8M-$2.6M, n=11) to maintain a published frontier safety framework among developer members above $500M revenue.
- 86 responding members; not a probability sample.

## Landscape facts (checked 22 Oct 2026)

- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act): signed Sept. 29, 2025; in effect Jan. 1, 2026; 15-day critical safety incident reporting to Cal OES, 24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026; effective Jan. 1, 2027; 72-hour incident reporting; annual third-party reviews.
- Illinois SB 315 (AI Safety Measures Act): signed July 6, 2026; effective Jan. 1, 2027; annual independent audit from Jan. 1, 2028.
- Dec. 2025 EO "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence": DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce evaluation of state AI laws.
- White House National Policy Framework legislative recommendations, March 20, 2026: preempt state AI laws imposing "undue burdens"; "a minimally burdensome national standard."
- EO 14409 (June 2, 2026): voluntary pre-release engagement with covered frontier models; expressly disclaims mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting for new models.

"}

Anticipated questions from Hill meetings (Sep 2026). Answers are 120 words or fewer. Section cites are to the June 4, 2026, discussion draft.

## 1. Majority E&C staff: If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.

We do not oppose incident reporting. We oppose the definition. Sec. 101(7) makes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" reportable with no harm requirement, which is broader than the state laws. Reporting should turn on demonstrated harms: actual death, serious injury, major property damage or actual critical-infrastructure compromise. On timing we agree with the draft: 15 days, matching SB 53, plus the 24-hour imminent-danger channel. Resist any move toward New York's 72-hour clock. A federal duty is lighter than the status quo only if it replaces the state duties, which is why we want Sec. 121 durable, with confidentiality for reports and a good-faith safe harbor. Dual SB 53 and RAISE compliance costs our members a median of 6.5 FTEs.

## 2. Minority staff (Trahan-aligned): Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?

A concrete list. We support published frontier AI frameworks for large frontier developers, Sec. 111(a); transparency reports at deployment, Sec. 111(c); 15-day incident reporting keyed to demonstrated harm; whistleblower anti-retaliation protections, Sec. 113; the GAO review of model-weight security, Sec. 321; and CAISI's voluntary standards work, Sec. 102. Our developer members above the $500 million threshold already maintain published frameworks, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year. What we cannot accept is obligations keyed to speculative catastrophic-risk scenarios instead of demonstrated harms. That distinction, harms versus hypotheses, is our line. Write the federal regime to real harms and we will support it and defend it to our startups.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: Three years or permanent, what is the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?

Permanent, if the votes exist. At minimum, extended, with the federal standard reauthorized and in place before any sunset. The draft's three-year clock is shorter than a data-center buildout; our members plan capital on five- to ten-year horizons. As structured, Secs. 111 and 112 sunset and Sec. 121 preemption lapses in the same window, so year three returns the country to the patchwork mid-investment. That is a cliff, not a framework. The Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 rejected a blanket 10-year moratorium, not the narrower, development-focused preemption in this draft, which the White House's March 20 framework also supports.

## 4. Appropriations staff: CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What is your view on the funding level?

{"content":"# One National Standard for AI Development

**ACIA on the Great American AI Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan), House Energy & Commerce**

**Bottom line.** ACIA, a coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms, supports the draft's core: one national standard for AI model development instead of a fifty-state patchwork. With five targeted fixes, our members will support it enthusiastically.

**Why it matters.** Three frontier-AI statutes landed in eighteen months: California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315, each with its own definitions, clocks and enforcement. In ACIA's August member survey (86 responding members), 61% named conflicting state definitions their top compliance problem, 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York last year, and developers complying with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 FTEs. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. The patchwork is a moat around the largest incumbents.

## ACIA's five asks

**1. Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** The development-focused scope is right and we support it. But Secs. 111 and 112 sunset and preemption lapses in the same three-year window: in year three the standard disappears and states return mid-buildout. Compute investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is a countdown, not a standard. At minimum, extend preemption with the federal standard reauthorized and in place before any sunset.

**2. Define "critical safety incident" by demonstrated harm (Sec. 101(7)).** As drafted, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" or "loss of control" is reportable with no one harmed. Speculative catastrophic-risk scenarios are not a sound basis for legislation. Require actual death, serious injury, major property damage or actual critical-infrastructure compromise.

**3. Keep the 15-day reporting window (Sec. 111(f)-(g)).** The draft matches SB 53's 15 days plus a 24-hour imminent-danger channel. Do not follow New York's 72-hour clock or the separate seven-day bill. Short clocks produce noise, not information.

**4. Protect good-faith reporters (Secs. 111(g), (i)).** Extend the draft's own FOIA exemption (5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), as in Sec. 102) to incident reports, and add a safe harbor so an honest report cannot be used as evidence of a violation. Penalties now reach $1 million per violation, per day.

**5. Keep CAISI voluntary and right-size audits (Secs. 102, 112).** Support codification and the voluntary standards mission; oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority or release gate, consistent with EO 14409's no-gate language. Move IVO audits to an annual, compliance-focused cadence; semi-annual is heavier than any state law it would replace.

**Also support:** NAIRR, AI testbeds, international standards coalitions excluding China, CISA open-source grants, GAO model-weight review.

**Contact:** Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.
","path":"/workspace/out/hill_one_pager.md"}

{"content":"# ACIA Files Comment on the Great American AI Act

On Monday ACIA submitted comment to Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan on their Great American AI Act discussion draft, after sign-off by President and CEO Grant Holloway.

The draft gets the big question right: one national standard for AI model development instead of a fifty-state patchwork. Our letter strongly supports its federalization provision and asks that it be made permanent, with the federal standard in place before any sunset.

Where we ask for changes: a narrower, harm-based "critical safety incident" definition; a preserved 15-day reporting window; confidentiality and a good-faith safe harbor for incident reports; and a voluntary CAISI, not a pre-deployment gatekeeper.

The letter leads with our August member survey: 61% of members cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York.

Questions or to join the working group: Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy.
","path":"/workspace/out/newsletter_blurb.md"}

{"path":"/workspace/out/staff_qa.md","content":"# Staff Q&A: GAAIA Discussion Draft

Anticipated questions from Hill meetings (Sep 2026). Answers are 120 words or fewer. Section cites are to the June 4, 2026, discussion draft.

## 1. Majority E&C staff: If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.

We do not oppose incident reporting. We oppose the definition. Sec. 101(7) makes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" reportable with no harm requirement, broader than the state laws. Reporting should turn on demonstrated harms: actual death, serious injury, major property damage or actual critical-infrastructure compromise. On timing we agree with the draft: 15 days, matching SB 53, plus the 24-hour imminent-danger channel. Resist any move toward New York's 72-hour clock. A federal duty is only lighter if it replaces the state duties, which is why we want Sec. 121 durable, with confidentiality and a good-faith safe harbor. Parallel SB 53 and RAISE compliance costs a median of 6.5 FTEs.

## 2. Minority staff (Trahan-aligned): Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?

A concrete list. We support published frontier AI frameworks for large frontier developers, Sec. 111(a); transparency reports at deployment, Sec. 111(c); 15-day incident reporting keyed to demonstrated harm; whistleblower anti-retaliation protections, Sec. 113; the GAO review of model-weight security, Sec. 321; and CAISI's voluntary standards work, Sec. 102. Our developer members above the $500 million threshold already maintain published frameworks, at a median cost of $1.4 million a year. What we cannot accept is obligations keyed to speculative catastrophic-risk scenarios instead of demonstrated harms. That distinction, harms versus hypotheses, is our line. Write the federal regime to real harms and we will support it and defend it to our startups.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: Three years or permanent, what is the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?

Permanent, if the votes exist. At minimum, extended, with the federal standard reauthorized and in place before any sunset. The draft's three-year clock is shorter than a data-center buildout; our members plan capital on five- to ten-year horizons. As structured, Secs. 111 and 112 sunset and Sec. 121 preemption lapses in the same window, so year three returns the country to the patchwork mid-investment. That is a cliff, not a framework. The Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 rejected a blanket 10-year moratorium, not the narrower, development-focused preemption in this draft, which the White House's March 20 framework also supports.

## 4. Appropriations staff: CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What is your view on the funding level?

No position on the topline; that is our board-approved holding. Three observations for appropriators. First, context: the sponsors note $100 million is roughly ten times CAISI's current appropriation of about $15 million. Second, fund the mission we support: voluntary standards, evaluation and monitoring, plus Title IV's testbeds and NAIRR. We oppose funding any mandatory pre-deployment testing gate. Third, watch the fee authority. The draft funds CAISI partly through fees on IVOs and large frontier developers, a pass-through cost on the regulated. Appropriations should carry the load where possible, and the GAO reviews in Secs. 122 and 321 provide regular oversight of what the center delivers.
"}

# ACIA Comment Letter: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act Discussion Draft

**DRAFT for President & CEO sign-off (ACIA-POL-2026-117). Not sent. To be transmitted to GAAIA@mail.house.gov.**

---

[ACIA LETTERHEAD]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: ACIA comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for the open process you have run since releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act on June 4, and for the bipartisan example you have set with Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of roughly 140 members: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the silicon and the compute infrastructure on which American AI leadership depends. We write to endorse the draft's central architecture and to request specific changes before introduction.

Our positions in brief. We strongly support the federalization provision in Sec. 121 and ask that it be made permanent, or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before any sunset. We oppose the critical safety incident provisions as drafted, Secs. 101(7) and 111(f)-(g), for four fixable reasons. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) with a voluntary standards mission under Sec. 102, and we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority added as the bill moves. We take no position on the $100 million annual authorization.

## I. The patchwork is not a hypothetical. It is a line item.

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by the chapter amendment signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, phases in through 2028. Three frontier-AI statutes in three states inside eighteen months, each with its own definitions, reporting clocks, audit expectations and enforcement apparatus, aimed at the same handful of nationally operating developers.

Our members are living with the results. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of our startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past twelve months because of state AI rules. Our developer members that must comply with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on dual compliance. Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median of $310,000 before the first report is ever filed, and our developer members above the draft's $500 million revenue threshold spend a median of $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

These costs are not evenly shared. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, which do not have compliance departments. The largest incumbents can absorb fifty state regimes and, candidly, benefit from the moat. That is why ACIA's members, competitors in nearly everything, are united on this: one clear federal standard, light-touch and risk-based, beats a fifty-state patchwork.

We endorse the finding in Sec. 121 that the development of AI models is "a matter of national economic significance and international competitiveness requiring uniform Federal oversight." The direction matches the executive branch's own posture. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20 legislative framework asked Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose "undue burdens" in favor of "a minimally burdensome national standard." Your draft is the vehicle.

## II. Preemption: make the standard durable

The draft's federalization provision is well scoped. It reaches state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models, where the conflicts are sharpest, and leaves states their traditional authority over deployment, use and laws of general applicability, along with common-law remedies. That balance is right. We support it.

Our concern is the clock. The obligations in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment, and the federalization provision lapses in the same window unless reauthorized. Year three is therefore the worst possible outcome: the federal standard disappears, the states return, and companies that spent three years building to a federal specification start over. Compute and data-center investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is not a standard. It is a countdown.

Requested change: make Sec. 121 permanent. If permanence is not achievable in this Congress, extend the provision and require reauthorization of the federal standard well before any sunset, so that at no point does the country revert to the patchwork the draft was written to end.

## III. Incident reporting: oppose as drafted, with four fixes

ACIA does not oppose incident reporting in principle. Our members already run disclosure and escalation processes under SB 53 and are preparing for RAISE. What we cannot support is the draft's definition of what must be reported.

Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a frontier model, with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed. Under that definition, a mitigation that underperforms an internal threshold becomes a federal reportable event. Catastrophic-risk scenarios of this kind are 
... [722 chars truncated] ...
24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury mirror SB 53, and we support them. Resist any pressure to conform to New York's 72-hour clock, and note that separate proposals in Congress would set clocks as short as seven days. Shorter windows do not produce better information. They produce hurried, lawyer-driven over-reporting that buries the regulator in noise, and with it the genuinely serious incidents the regime exists to catch.

3. **Extend the draft's own confidentiality protections to incident reports.** Sec. 102 already exempts information shared with the Center from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) and bars its reuse by other regulators. Incident reports will necessarily describe security-sensitive details, including vulnerabilities. Publishing or leaking them would create the very risks the provision is meant to prevent. Please confirm the reporting subsection inherits those protections, and if it does not, add parallel language to Sec. 111.

4. **Add a safe harbor for good-faith reports.** Sec. 111(i) sets penalties at up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately. At that exposure, an honest report of a marginal event hands the government its case, and silence becomes the rational strategy. That is backwards. A good-faith report should not be usable as evidence of a violation, and penalties for non-willful, procedural violations should be tiered and preceded by notice and an opportunity to cure.

## IV. Verification and audits: restructure Sec. 112

The independent verification organization (IVO) regime is the heaviest single provision in the draft. Large frontier developers must retain CAISI-licensed auditors, grant them timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with mandatory referral to federal and state attorneys general where an IVO perceives "imminent catastrophic risk."

Two problems. Semi-annual audits are heavier than any state regime the draft would replace; New York and Illinois each settled on annual review cycles. And the IVO's mandate is keyed not to compliance but to whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," an open-ended invitation to second-guess engineering judgment against speculative scenarios.

Requested changes: align the audit cadence to annual; scope audits to verification of the developer's compliance with its published framework and with the Act; protect audit materials with the same confidentiality as Sec. 102 information; limit ad hoc audits to articulable facts rather than hypotheticals; and tie mandatory referrals to imminent, demonstrated harm.

## V. CAISI: a voluntary mission

We support codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce under Sec. 102, with the substantial capacity the draft would give it for voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring. This builds on recommendations of the House AI Task Force and mirrors the administration's approach. Executive Order 14409 of June 2 establishes voluntary pre-release engagement with covered frontier models and expressly disclaims any "mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement" for new models.

Two requests. First, keep CAISI's evaluation work voluntary, collaborative and confidential, and write EO 14409's no-gate language into the statute. Second, we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, or any release gate, added as the draft moves. The center's value to industry and government is technical credibility, not veto power. On the $100 million annual authorization we take no position. We note only that the draft's fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers passes costs through to the regulated.

## VI. Provisions we support

**Sec. 111(a) and (c):** published frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports, with the revenue floors in Sec. 101 and the redaction authority for trade secrets, cybersecurity and national security intact. Disclosure at the scale of the largest developers is workable; our members above the threshold already do it, at a median of $1.4 million a year.

**Sec. 113:** whistleblower anti-retaliation protections, which we support. One clarification: "AI violation" should be defined by reference to violations of this Act, not of any federal statute touching AI, so the provision does not become a roving federal cause of action.

**Secs. 401, 411, 423, 311, 321 and 132:** the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST; international standards coalitions that exclude China; codification of the National AI Research Resource; CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; the GAO review of model-weight and data-center security; and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support all of them. They invest in the innovation side of the ledger, which is where America wins.

## VII. Conclusion

The Great American AI Act asks the right question: whether the United States will govern frontier AI under one national standard or fifty discordant ones. ACIA's answer is the same one we gave OSTP in our March 2025 comment on the AI Action Plan: preempt the patchwork. As drafted, the bill would do that, but on a clock too short to bank investment against, and with a reporting definition that treats speculative scenarios as reportable events.

Our members would support enthusiastically a bill that does the following: one national standard, light-touch and risk-based, keyed to demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones, and durable enough to plan against. We stand ready to help you write it.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Questions and offers of technical assistance may be directed to Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President and CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

**ACIA on the Great American AI Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan), House Energy & Commerce**

**Bottom line.** ACIA, a coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms, supports the draft's core: one national standard for AI model development instead of a fifty-state patchwork. **Why it matters.** Three frontier-AI statutes landed in eighteen months: California SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315, each with its own definitions, clocks and enforcement. In ACIA's August member survey (86 responding members), 61% named conflicting state definitions their top compliance problem, 34% of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York last year, and developers complying with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 FTEs. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. The patchwork is a moat around the largest incumbents.

**1. Make preemption permanent (Sec. 121).** The development-focused scope is right and we support it. But Secs. 111 and 112 sunset and preemption lapses in the same three-year window: in year three the standard disappears and states return mid-buildout. Compute investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is a countdown, not a standard. **2. Define "critical safety incident" by demonstrated harm (Sec. 101(7)).** As drafted, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" or "loss of control" is reportable with no one harmed. # ACIA Comment Letter: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act Discussion Draft

**DRAFT for President & CEO sign-off (ACIA-POL-2026-117). Not sent. To be transmitted to GAAIA@mail.house.gov.**

---

[ACIA LETTERHEAD]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: ACIA comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for the open process you have run since releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act on June 4, and for the bipartisan example you have set with Reps. Scott Franklin, Suhas Subramanyam, Erin Houchin and Scott Peters. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of roughly 140 members: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the silicon and the compute infrastructure on which American AI leadership depends. We write to endorse the draft's central architecture and to request specific changes before introduction.

Our positions in brief. We strongly support the federalization provision in Sec. 121 and ask that it be made permanent, or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before any sunset. We oppose the critical safety incident provisions as drafted, Secs. 101(7) and 111(f)-(g), for four fixable reasons. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) with a voluntary standards mission under Sec. 102, and we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority added as the bill moves. We take no position on the $100 million annual authorization.

## I. The patchwork is not a hypothetical. It is a line item.

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by the chapter amendment signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315), signed July 6, phases in through 2028. Three frontier-AI statutes in three states inside eighteen months, each with its own definitions, reporting clocks, audit expectations and enforcement apparatus, aimed at the same handful of nationally operating developers.

Our members are living with the results. In ACIA's August 2026 member survey (86 responding members; not a probability sample), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their single biggest compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of our startup members reported delaying a product launch in California or New York in the past twelve months because of state AI rules. Our developer members that must comply with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel spend a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents on dual compliance. Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median of $310,000 before the first report is ever filed, and our developer members above the draft's $500 million revenue threshold spend a median of $1.4 million a year maintaining a published frontier safety framework.

These costs are not evenly shared. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, which do not have compliance departments. The largest incumbents can absorb fifty state regimes and, candidly, benefit from the moat. That is why ACIA's members, competitors in nearly everything, are united on this: one clear federal standard, light-touch and risk-based, beats a fifty-state patchwork.

We endorse the finding in Sec. 121 that the development of AI models is "a matter of national economic significance and international competitiveness requiring uniform Federal oversight." The direction matches the executive branch's own posture. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force to challenge burdensome state laws, and the White House's March 20 legislative framework asked Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose "undue burdens" in favor of "a minimally burdensome national standard." Your draft is the vehicle.

## II. Preemption: make the standard durable

The draft's federalization provision is well scoped. It reaches state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models, where the conflicts are sharpest, and leaves states their traditional authority over deployment, use and laws of general applicability, along with common-law remedies. That balance is right. We support it.

Our concern is the clock. The obligations in Secs. 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment, and the federalization provision lapses in the same window unless reauthorized. Year three is therefore the worst possible outcome: the federal standard disappears, the states return, and companies that spent three years building to a federal specification start over. Compute and data-center investment runs on five- to ten-year horizons. A three-year truce is not a standard. It is a countdown.

Requested change: make Sec. 121 permanent. If permanence is not achievable in this Congress, extend the provision and require reauthorization of the federal standard well before any sunset, so that at no point does the country revert to the patchwork the draft was written to end.

## III. Incident reporting: oppose as drafted, with four fixes

ACIA does not oppose incident reporting in principle. Our members already run disclosure and escalation processes under SB 53 and are preparing for RAISE. What we cannot support is the draft's definition of what must be reported.

Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" of a frontier model, with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed. Under that definition, a mitigation that underperforms an internal threshold becomes a federal reportable event. Catastrophic-risk scenarios of this kind are speculative, and speculative risks are not a sound basis for legislation. A federal reporting regime should be keyed to demonstrated harms.

We ask for four changes.

1. **Narrow the definition.** A reportable incident under Sec. 101(7) should require demonstrated harm: actual death, serious bodily injury, significant property damage or actual compromise of critical infrastructure, arising from a frontier model. Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights is a concrete security event and is appropriately reportable. The failure and loss-of-control prongs, as drafted, would import scenario analysis into a regulatory filing.

2. **Preserve the 15-day window.** The draft's 15-day reporting clock and its 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury mirror SB 53, and we support them. Resist any pressure to conform to New York's 72-hour clock, and note that separate proposals in Congress would set clocks as short as seven days. Shorter windows do not produce better information. They produce hurried, lawyer-driven over-reporting that buries the regulator in noise, and with it the genuinely serious incidents the regime exists to catch.

3. **Extend the draft's own confidentiality protections to incident reports.** Sec. 102 already exempts information shared with the Center from disclosure under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3) and bars its reuse by other regulators. Incident reports will necessarily describe security-sensitive details, including vulnerabilities. Publishing or leaking them would create the very risks the provision is meant to prevent. Please confirm the reporting subsection inherits those protections, and if it does not, add parallel language to Sec. 111.

4. **Add a safe harbor for good-faith reports.** Sec. 111(i) sets penalties at up to $1 million per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately. At that exposure, an honest report of a marginal event hands the government its case, and silence becomes the rational strategy. That is backwards. A good-faith report should not be usable as evidence of a violation, and penalties for non-willful, procedural violations should be tiered and preceded by notice and an opportunity to cure.

## IV. Verification and audits: restructure Sec. 112

The independent verification organization (IVO) regime is the heaviest single provision in the draft. Large frontier developers must retain CAISI-licensed auditors, grant them timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and submit to semi-annual audits plus ad hoc audits at the Director's request, with mandatory referral to federal and state attorneys general where an IVO perceives "imminent catastrophic risk."

Two problems. Semi-annual audits are heavier than any state regime the draft would replace; New York and Illinois each settled on annual review cycles. And the IVO's mandate is keyed not to compliance but to whether a developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," an open-ended invitation to second-guess engineering judgment against speculative scenarios.

Requested changes: align the audit cadence to annual; scope audits to verification of the developer's compliance with its published framework and with the Act; protect audit materials with the same confidentiality as Sec. 102 information; limit ad hoc audits to articulable facts rather than hypotheticals; and tie mandatory referrals to imminent, demonstrated harm.

## V. CAISI: a voluntary mission

We support codifying CAISI within the Department of Commerce under Sec. 102, with the substantial capacity the draft would give it for voluntary guidelines, standards, evaluation and monitoring. This builds on recommendations of the House AI Task Force and mirrors the administration's approach. Executive Order 14409 of June 2 establishes voluntary pre-release engagement with covered frontier models and expressly disclaims any "mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement" for new models.

Two requests. First, keep CAISI's evaluation work voluntary, collaborative and confidential, and write EO 14409's no-gate language into the statute. Second, we would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, or any release gate, added as the draft moves. The center's value to industry and government is technical credibility, not veto power. On the $100 million annual authorization we take no position. We note only that the draft's fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers passes costs through to the regulated.

## VI. Provisions we support

**Sec. 111(a) and (c):** published frontier AI frameworks and transparency reports, with the revenue floors in Sec. 101 and the redaction authority for trade secrets, cybersecurity and national security intact. Disclosure at the scale of the largest developers is workable; our members above the threshold already do it, at a median of $1.4 million a year.

**Sec. 113:** whistleblower anti-retaliation protections, which we support. One clarification: "AI violation" should be defined by reference to violations of this Act, not of any federal statute touching AI, so the provision does not become a roving federal cause of action.

**Secs. 401, 411, 423, 311, 321 and 132:** the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy and NIST; international standards coalitions that exclude China; codification of the National AI Research Resource; CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; the GAO review of model-weight and data-center security; and penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials. We support all of them. They invest in the innovation side of the ledger, which is where America wins.

## VII. Conclusion

The Great American AI Act asks the right question: whether the United States will govern frontier AI under one national standard or fifty discordant ones. ACIA's answer is the same one we gave OSTP in our March 2025 comment on the AI Action Plan: preempt the patchwork. As drafted, the bill would do that, but on a clock too short to bank investment against, and with a reporting definition that treats speculative scenarios as reportable events.

Our members would support enthusiastically a bill that does the following: one national standard, light-touch and risk-based, keyed to demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones, and durable enough to plan against. We stand ready to help you write it.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. Questions and offers of technical assistance may be directed to Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President and CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
